text: Every hunt in this chapter has pointed toward this moment. A hypothesis formed, run through the loop, sourced systematically from ATT&CK coverage gaps -- and now one of those hunts actually confirms something real: the rundll32.exe hypothesis turns up a genuine malicious launch on a real host, not just a clean result.

A hunting query only runs when an analyst manually decides to run it. If that exact pattern shows up again next week, nothing catches it unless someone happens to hunt for the same thing again. A confirmed finding an analyst has to manually re-check for, forever, is exactly the kind of gap a mature hunting program closes.

The Sentinel course already covered the Scheduled Analytics Rule: one KQL query plus run frequency, lookback window, and alert threshold. A successful hunt already did the hardest part -- it has a query proven against real data. Converting it means taking that same query into Analytics, Create, Scheduled query rule, so it runs automatically instead of waiting on an analyst's memory.

The query's core logic usually doesn't change much -- it already proved it works. What needs deliberate attention is the scheduling: lookback set longer than run frequency, per the Sentinel course's own guidance, to avoid an ingestion-delay gap, and a threshold reflecting genuine risk rather than just the one host from the hunt.

This is the real payoff this whole chapter has built toward. A hypothesis sourced from an ATT&CK coverage gap, run through the hunting loop, confirmed real, and converted into an automated rule means that specific gap in detection coverage is now permanently closed -- Sentinel catches it on its own schedule from here on.

That's the concrete difference between a SOC that hunts occasionally and one where hunting measurably improves the baseline over time, hunt after hunt. Next: the Job-Ready Capstone begins, putting the full incident response lifecycle to work on one real, end-to-end exercise.
